blocks.text: Imagine a self-driving car navigating through busy city streets. It must make split-second decisions to ensure safety. How does its operating system prioritize tasks to meet strict deadlines?

blocks.markdown: In real-time systems, tasks must be completed within specific time constraints. These constraints can be categorized as either hard or soft real-time requirements. Understanding these distinctions is crucial for designing systems that meet their operational needs.

blocks.title: Hard vs. Soft Real-Time Requirements
blocks.text: Hard real-time systems require tasks to be completed within a strict deadline, where missing the deadline could lead to catastrophic failure. Soft real-time systems have more flexible deadlines, where missing a deadline may degrade performance but not cause a complete system failure.

blocks.markdown: Rate-monotonic scheduling (RMS) is a common algorithm used in real-time systems. It assigns priorities to tasks based on their periodicity: the more frequent the task, the higher its priority.

blocks.title: Rate-Monotonic Scheduling
blocks.text: In RMS, tasks are assigned priorities according to their frequency. Higher frequency tasks have higher priority, making RMS optimal for fixed-priority scheduling of periodic tasks.

blocks.markdown: In multiprocessor systems, scheduling becomes more complex due to the need to distribute tasks across multiple cores. Two important concepts here are load balancing and processor affinity.

blocks.title: Load Balancing and Processor Affinity
blocks.text: Load balancing ensures that tasks are evenly distributed across processors to optimize performance. Processor affinity refers to the tendency of a process to run on a specific processor, which can improve cache performance by keeping data local to a processor.

blocks.title: Scheduling Complexity
blocks.text: Scheduling on multiprocessor systems is NP-hard, meaning that finding an optimal solution can be computationally expensive.

points: Real-time systems require tasks to be completed within specific deadlines, with hard and soft real-time requirements defining the level of strictness.
Rate-monotonic scheduling assigns priorities based on task frequency and is optimal for fixed-priority scheduling of periodic tasks.
In multiprocessor systems, load balancing and processor affinity are key to optimizing performance.
